title: You can be Moses (Teshuvah 5:2)
hookLine: every person can become righteous like Moses or wicked like Jeroboam
last: TESHUVAH: RECOGNIZE, REGRET, CONFESS, RESOLVE, REPAIR.

cards: Two names sit side by side in a law book. One is Moses, who stood on the mountain and brought down the Torah. The other is Jeroboam, a king of Israel who set up golden calves and led people away.
You might expect a writer to put them at opposite ends of the universe, made of different stuff. Maimonides does something stranger.
In the middle of his laws of return, he puts the two names in the same sentence, and he puts you between them. Either one, he says, is open to you.

teach.h: EVERY PERSON CAN TURN EITHER WAY.
teach.b: You can be Moses. It's from the fifth chapter of the Laws of Repentance in the Mishneh Torah. First, the claim.
Permission is given to every human being, Maimonides writes. Want to turn toward the good way and be righteous? You can.
Toward the bad way? You can. Every person can be righteous like Moses our teacher, or wicked like Jeroboam.
Wise or foolish, merciful or cruel. Second, what he's pushing against.
He calls foolish the idea that God decrees at birth whether a person will be righteous or wicked. Nobody forces a person, nobody decrees it, nobody drags them down either road. The person chooses.
Third, why it sits here. If your character were fixed at birth, regret would be pointless and resolve would be theater.
Return only works if the road can change direction.

He calls this freedom a great principle, a pillar of the Torah and the commandments, and grounds it in Deuteronomy, where life and good, death and evil, are set before the people, and the call comes: "therefore choose life."

If God knows everything ahead of time, how can a person really choose? He doesn't wave it away. The answer is beyond human understanding, he says, because God's knowing is not like ours, and he holds on to both.
God knows, and you choose. Readers have argued about that answer.
But the sentence about Moses stands either way. Nothing written at your birth closes the road.

how: Some Jews study the Mishneh Torah's Laws of Repentance, including chapter five on free choice, in the season before Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, when return is the theme.

games.q: what does “you can be moses” mean?
o: only a prophet can rise to the level of Moses
a blessing that every child grow up to lead Israel
every person is free to choose; nothing is fixed at birth

games.q: you can be moses — tap the pairs.

s: Maimonides teaches that some people are born to be righteous
he calls that idea foolish. nobody decrees it; the person chooses.
his teaching on free choice sits inside the laws of repentance
it's in the fifth chapter of the Laws of Repentance, because return needs a road that can change.
he claims to fully explain how God's knowledge fits with free choice
he says the answer is beyond human understanding, and holds on to both.

games.q: you're Maimonides. a student asks: if God already knows what I'll do, how am I free? what do you answer?
o: God's knowing is beyond us; God knows, and you choose.
games.why: he refuses to give up either side. God's knowledge isn't like ours, he says, so we can't grasp how they fit, but both are true.

practice: Notice the small choices already in this moment: whether to keep sitting, whether to follow a thought or let it go, whether to breathe a little slower.
Then think of one moment in your day where you usually run on autopilot, the reply you always give, the scroll you always start, and decide freely what you'd do there instead.
If you pray, you can hold the words "therefore choose life" for a breath.

wordCard.voice: You can be Moses. Maimonides' teaching that every person is free to become righteous like Moses or wicked like Jeroboam, and nothing at birth decides it. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: permission, authority. Maimonides says this 'permission' to choose is given to every human being.

carryVoice: Your line: you can be moses. Either road is open, and the choosing is yours. See you tomorrow.
